newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia cuts rates, sees lower yields.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia cuts rates, sees lower yields.

text.p: Russia's central bank announced on Thursday it was cutting its main interest rate and forecast further falls in yields on government paper later this year.

The news immediately pushed up prices of GKO discount Treasury bills and OFZ interest-bearing government bonds, with the average yield falling to 29.29 percent from 30.45 percent on Tuesday, the previous trading day.

But a senior central bank official also warned that the huge volume of foreign investment in government securities, which has helped drive down yields over the past nine months, was making it harder for the authorities to manage the market.
The central bank said it was cutting its refinancing rate from April 28 to 36 percent, the lowest level for more than five years, from the 42 percent in force since February 10.
The central bank does not actually use the refinancing rate as the basis for any lending facility to commercial banks.
But the rate, widely used in contracts and setting commercial bank rates, is an important indicator, and T-bill prices rose on the news.

"Market participants have received the regular confirmation that yields are unlikely to go up. Prices are rising, with the rate of growth rising in proportion to the length of maturity of each issue," said Oleg Gorbonosov of brokers C.A. & Co.
The central bank, which also cut the rates it uses on its Lombard lending facility to banks, did not give any reason for the refinancing rate move.

But T-bill yields have been falling recently and inflation has continued to slow. The monthly price rise is officially forecast at 1.3 percent in April after 1.4 percent in March and 2.2 percent in April last year.
On Tuesday Central Bank Chairman Sergei Dubinin said the bank aimed to cut the refinancing rate to about 25 percent over an unspecified period.

The authorities are keen to see interest rates fall, so that companies will be able to borrow, helping the economic recovery, and banks will be encouraged to lend to industry instead of investing in high-yielding government securities.

Yields have fallen to just over 30 percent from over 200 percent early last year, and since last summer the authorities have merely been rolling over debt in the government securities market, not borrowing new money, to encourage the fall.

A senior central bank official said the government would now shift the emphasis in its borrowing foreign markets from the domestic market with the aim of getting yields down to 20-25 percent in the second half of this year.

"That is the minimum level at which interest from both Russian and foreign investors can be preserved," Konstantin Korishchenko, head of the bank's open-market operations department, told an investment conference.
Russia successfully placed a two billion mark Eurobond in March after its heavily oversubscribed debut $1 billion Eurobond last November.
It plans to return to international capital markets in the next few months.
But foreign investors have also been keen buyers of Treaury bills, helping drive down yields.
Korishchenko said foreigners had invested $11 billion in Russian government securities since August last year, and now accounted for more daily activity on the domestic market than local investors.
Non-residents now hold about 20 percent of the Russian government securities market, whose volume is $45-50 billion, Korishchenko said.

This large involvement is already making it harder for the authorities to manage the market. Korishchenko said the authorities were continuing to liberalise foreign access to the market, but would retain the ability to limit foreign capital inflows.

The Central Bank has announced a staged liberalisation of the market, which will remove all restrictions on foreigners repatriating profits from the government securities market by the end of the year.
